content.title: AI CCTV for Banks, ATMs & BFSI in Mumbai (2026 Compliance Guide)

children.text: AI CCTV for banks and ATMs in Mumbai delivers round-the-clock branch monitoring, real-time fraud and tailgating alerts, encrypted audit-ready footage, and a unified dashboard across every location in a financial institution's network. For Mumbai's banks, NBFCs, cooperative lenders, and financial services firms operating under regulatory scrutiny, intelligent surveillance is both a security necessity and a compliance asset — ensuring incidents are detected early, evidence is preserved reliably, and oversight is always available to authorised personnel.
Why Does Mumbai's BFSI Sector Need Intelligent Surveillance?

Mumbai is India's financial capital. The city hosts the headquarters of public and private sector banks, the Reserve Bank of India, major NBFCs, insurance companies, asset management firms, and thousands of ATM kiosks spread across every neighbourhood from Nariman Point to Navi Mumbai.

That concentration of financial assets, cash-handling infrastructure, and sensitive customer data creates a security environment that is categorically different from retail or commercial premises. A branch premises is not just a place of business — it is a regulated entity with documented obligations around physical security, evidence retention, and access control. An ATM vestibule handles cash transactions around the clock with minimal human presence. A regional processing centre may hold documents and data that require chain-of-custody assurance.

Conventional closed-circuit cameras record events. That matters. But Mumbai's BFSI operators increasingly need surveillance that does more: detecting a potential threat before it becomes an incident, capturing clear face images for investigation, alerting security teams the moment an after-hours intrusion is detected, and delivering footage that an auditor or investigator can access — in the right format, with the right timestamps — without delay.
AI-powered surveillance closes that gap.
What Are the Core Security and Compliance Needs for BFSI Surveillance?
How Should a Bank Branch Monitor Its Premises for Safety and Fraud?

A modern bank branch hosts tellers, customer service desks, loan processing areas, safe rooms, and public waiting zones — each with different access permissions and risk profiles. Effective branch surveillance must handle all of them simultaneously.
ArcisAI's edge AI cameras deliver real-time detection across these zones:

• Intrusion detection — alerts the security team immediately when anyone enters a restricted area, such as the server room, document vault, or employee-only back office, outside authorised hours or without proper access.
• Human and crowd detection — identifies when an unusual number of people gather near a teller counter or ATM lobby, flagging potential duress situations or suspicious queue management.

• Loitering detection — raises an alert when an individual lingers in a branch entrance, ATM vestibule, or car park beyond a configurable time threshold — a known early indicator of surveillance activity before a crime.
• Abandoned object detection — flags unattended bags, packages, or devices left in customer-facing areas, critical in any high-footfall financial premises.

• After-hours alerts — any human presence detected in a branch or ATM enclosure during closed hours triggers an instant notification to the security operations centre or branch manager's mobile device.

All of these detections run on-device at the camera edge, meaning they fire in real time without depending on a stable internet uplink — and without sending raw video streams continuously to the cloud.
What Surveillance Capabilities Are Specifically Important for ATM Monitoring?

ATM kiosks are among the most targeted financial infrastructure in any city. Cash-filled, often located in low-footfall locations at night, and sometimes staffed by a single security guard for limited hours — they present a distinct set of surveillance requirements.
AI CCTV addresses ATM security across several dimensions:

• Face capture and recognition — cameras positioned at ATM entry points capture high-quality facial images of users. Where lawfully applicable, face recognition can flag individuals of interest in real time. In all cases, the captured images support post-incident investigation.

• Tailgating detection — identifies when a second person follows an authorised user into a secured ATM vestibule without independent authentication, a common setup for card-skimming attacks and customer robbery.
• Line-crossing alerts — a virtual perimeter around the ATM machine itself triggers an alert if anyone reaches the defined boundary other than the customer actively transacting.
• 24/7 coverage with low-light capability — ArcisAI cameras function across challenging lighting conditions, ensuring coverage is consistent in night-time or poorly-lit ATM enclosures.

• ANPR for ATM drive-throughs and car park ATMs — automatic number plate recognition logs every vehicle approaching a drive-through or parking-area ATM, creating a verifiable record that supports investigation of card fraud or robbery.

How Does ArcisAI Support BFSI Compliance and Audit Readiness?
What Does Encrypted, Audit-Ready Footage Mean in Practice?

For a financial institution, recorded footage has a dual function: it is an operational security tool and a potential piece of evidence. When a customer dispute, an internal fraud investigation, a robbery, or a regulatory audit requires access to recordings, the footage must meet a higher standard than simply "existing."

ArcisAI's VMS is STQC-certified — assessed by the Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification directorate under India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. This certification covers the software's security architecture, including encrypted storage of recordings, role-based access permissions, and audit logs that record who accessed what footage and when.
In practice, this means:
• Footage is stored in an encrypted format that is tamper-evident — any unauthorised modification is detectable.

• Access to specific cameras, date ranges, or event clips is controlled by user role — a branch manager may see their own branch feeds; a regional security head may see all branches in their zone; an auditor may have read-only access to event logs.
• Every access action — login, clip download, footage export — is logged with timestamp and user identity, creating a chain of custody record for any exported evidence.
• Retention periods can be configured to meet institutional policy requirements.
Can BFSI Operators Choose Between Cloud, On-Premises, and Hybrid Deployment?

Yes. Financial institutions have varying data governance requirements. Some prefer all footage to remain on-premises within their own data centre; others are comfortable with a cloud-managed solution provided the servers are hosted in India. ArcisAI supports all three models:
• On-premises — NVR-based local recording with AI analytics running at the camera edge, no cloud dependency for core surveillance functions.
• Cloud — All analytics, storage, and dashboard access managed via ArcisAI's India-hosted cloud infrastructure.
• Hybrid — Edge AI for instant local alerts and on-prem NVR for local recording, combined with cloud VMS for multi-branch visibility, ArcisGPT forensic search, and centralised reporting.
The hybrid model is particularly well-suited to large BFSI networks: branches retain local resilience while the security operations centre gains enterprise-wide visibility from a single dashboard.
How Does ArcisAI Handle Multi-Branch Central Monitoring?

A bank with 50 branches across Mumbai — or a NBFC with offices from Andheri to Thane — cannot manage physical security with branch-level siloes. ArcisAI's cloud VMS aggregates all sites into one dashboard, accessible from the security operations centre, from a designated security head's desktop, or from any authorised mobile device.

ArcisGPT, ArcisAI's natural-language investigation interface, makes post-incident analysis significantly faster. Instead of instructing an operator to manually scrub through recordings, a security manager can query: "Show all intrusion alerts from the Bandra branch ATM between 11 PM and 3 AM last week" or "List all loitering detections at Dadar branch in the last 30 days" — and receive a filtered, timestamped result set in seconds. No specialist VMS training required.

content.title: AI CCTV for Factories & Warehouses: Safety, Security & Efficiency (2026)

children.text: AI-powered CCTV for factories and warehouses does far more than record incidents — it actively enforces PPE compliance, monitors loading bays, manages gate entry with ANPR, and gives plant managers a live, searchable view across every zone. For Indian industrial and logistics operators facing rising compliance pressures, labour safety mandates, and inventory leakage, an intelligent surveillance system is now a core operational tool, not a passive add-on.
Why Do Factories and Warehouses Need More Than Standard CCTV?
A conventional CCTV system answers one question: "What happened?" Industrial facilities need surveillance that answers a harder question: "What is happening right now — and does it need action?"

A forklift entering a no-go zone, a worker skipping a hard hat, a truck idling at a gate beyond its authorised window, an unattended package in a high-value aisle — these are live events, not historical footage. When alerts arrive in real time, supervisors can intervene before an accident, a theft, or a compliance breach becomes a reportable incident.

AI surveillance bridges that gap. On-device edge processing delivers instant detections without bandwidth overload. Cloud AI handles compute-intensive analytics — PPE recognition, vehicle classification, headcount — and feeds them into a unified dashboard accessible from any location. The result is a plant that is safer, more auditable, and far easier to manage across multiple sites.
What Industrial Safety Problems Can AI CCTV Solve?
How Does AI CCTV Enforce PPE Compliance on the Shop Floor?

Personal Protective Equipment non-compliance is one of the most common root causes of factory injuries, and one of the hardest to police manually when a facility operates across hundreds of square metres and multiple shifts.

ArcisAI's Cloud AI includes purpose-built PPE-kit detection: cameras continuously analyse whether workers in designated zones are wearing helmets, high-visibility vests, gloves, goggles, or other required protective equipment. When a violation is detected, the system:
• Sends an instant alert to the shift supervisor's mobile app.
• Logs a timestamped image for compliance records and audit trails.
• Accumulates shift-level and zone-level reports so safety managers can identify patterns — a specific entry point where violations cluster, or a particular shift where compliance drops.
No manual spot-check required. The camera watches every worker in its field of view, continuously, across every shift.
Can AI Cameras Detect Unauthorised Access and Perimeter Breaches?
Factories and warehouses carry significant risks from unauthorised entry — theft of raw materials, pilferage from loading areas, and safety hazards for visitors in live production zones.
ArcisAI edge AI cameras handle perimeter and internal access control with:
• Intrusion detection — alerts when a person or vehicle enters a restricted zone without authorisation.
• Line-crossing alerts — a virtual boundary triggers an instant notification the moment it is crossed, day or night.
• Human and vehicle detection — distinguishes people from animals or debris, reducing false alarms that create alert fatigue.
• Crowd detection — flags unusual gatherings near exits, sensitive equipment areas, or inventory zones.
These detections run directly on the camera hardware, so alerts reach the control room in seconds — even if the cloud connection is interrupted.
How Do AI Cameras Improve Loading Bay and Inventory Monitoring?
The loading bay is one of the highest-risk zones in any warehouse: high vehicle traffic, frequent handoffs, and limited supervisor presence during peak hours.
AI surveillance addresses this with:

• Vehicle classification and ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition) — identifies every truck or van entering and exiting the facility. Number plates are logged automatically, creating a verifiable record of arrivals, dwell times, and departures for every delivery and dispatch.
• Abandoned and missing object detection — flags when a pallet, package, or piece of equipment is left in an unexpected location, or when an expected item disappears from a monitored zone.
• Headcount analytics — tracks the number of personnel in loading areas in real time, supporting both safety compliance (maximum occupancy limits) and operational scheduling.

content.title: AI CCTV for Housing Societies & Gated Communities (2026 Guide)

children.text: AI CCTV for housing societies gives RWA committees automatic number plate recognition at the gate, digital visitor logging, perimeter intrusion alerts, and a mobile dashboard any committee member or guard can access in real time. Whether your society has 50 flats or 500, it makes daily security far more responsive than manual checks alone.
Why Is Traditional CCTV No Longer Enough for a Housing Society?

Most gated communities installed their first cameras years ago — fixed DVRs, low-resolution analog feeds, footage that nobody watches unless something has already gone wrong. That setup served a purpose, but residents and RWA committees are now managing far more complex security needs: delivery vehicles entering and leaving at all hours, multiple pedestrian gates, shared parking areas, play zones for children, and elderly residents who walk the grounds early in the morning.

The gap between what legacy cameras record and what communities actually need — proactive alerts, vehicle verification, visitor logs, remote access — is exactly where AI-powered surveillance makes its biggest difference. Rather than reviewing hours of footage after an incident, AI cameras detect and flag events as they happen, turning passive recording into an active safety layer for every resident.
What Security Challenges Do Housing Societies Face?
Before looking at solutions, it helps to name the problems RWA committees hear most often from residents.

Gate and entry management sits at the top of almost every list. Guards manually noting down vehicle numbers or checking visitor names on paper is slow, error-prone, and leaves no reliable audit trail. Delivery personnel, domestic workers, and vendors arrive throughout the day, and a single distracted guard moment is all it takes for an unauthorised person to slip through.

Perimeter security is equally pressing in large societies. Long boundary walls, poorly lit corners, and gaps in compound coverage create opportunities for trespass that residents may not discover until morning.

Parking misuse — unregistered vehicles occupying resident bays, unauthorised commercial vehicles entering — is a persistent source of conflict. And common-area incidents, from arguments near the clubhouse to medical emergencies near the swimming pool, rarely have a reliable record that can help the committee or police act quickly.
Finally, committee oversight is fragmented. The secretary or treasurer managing security from home has no visibility into what guards are actually doing unless they drive to the gate themselves.

How Does ANPR Work at a Society Gate?

ANPR — Automatic Number Plate Recognition — is one of the highest-value AI features a housing society can deploy at its entrance. A camera pointed at the vehicle approach lane reads the number plate in real time using cloud AI, then checks it against the society's registered vehicle database.

If the plate matches a resident's registered car, the guard dashboard can confirm entry automatically. If the plate is unrecognised — a visitor, a delivery van, or a commercial vehicle — the system flags it for manual check-in, and the visitor's details are logged digitally rather than on paper.

This creates a clean, searchable record. An RWA committee member can later open ArcisGPT — ArcisAI's natural-language search interface — and ask "show all unregistered vehicles at Gate 2 after 10 PM last week" and receive a filtered result without needing to scrub through recordings manually.

Yes. ArcisAI's cloud VMS is designed to aggregate feeds from multiple entry points — main gate, back gate, service entrance, parking boom barrier — into a single dashboard. Committee members with appropriate access can view any camera, review any alert, and manage the system from the mobile app whether they are inside the society or travelling.

For larger campuses, PTZ (pan-tilt-zoom) cameras on the grounds and along the perimeter can be paired with fixed Eco-Series cameras at gates and common areas. The PTZ cameras give guards the ability to track movement across open spaces — gardens, driveways, terraces — while the fixed cameras handle the high-throughput entry and exit points.
What Should an RWA Look for When Choosing a Society Security Camera?
Not every camera system marketed for housing societies delivers the same reliability or accountability. Here are the factors committees should evaluate before finalising a vendor.

Edge AI vs cloud-only processing. Cameras that send raw video to a distant server create latency and depend on a stable internet connection. Edge AI cameras process intrusion, human detection, and line-crossing alerts on the device itself, so guards receive instant alerts even if the internet is slow. Cloud AI handles heavier tasks — ANPR, face recognition where lawfully applicable.

Certifications and compliance. Look for cameras with BIS-ER certification (Bureau of Indian Standards, Electronics and IT Goods). ArcisAI Eco-Series cameras hold BIS-ER certification (R-72003735 ER01:2024). The VMS platform should carry STQC certification from India's Ministry of Electronics — ArcisAI's VMS is STQC-certified. Both matter for committees wanting to demonstrate compliance to residents and, if needed, to law enforcement.
Made in India and NDAA compliance. For societies seeking supply-chain assurance, Made in India hardware and NDAA-compliant products provide an additional layer of accountability.

Connectivity flexibility. Gate cameras may need PoE, a clubhouse camera WiFi, and a far perimeter corner 4G. ArcisAI's Eco-Series supports all three connectivity modes across 3MP, 5MP, and 8MP variants, so one product family covers the entire campus.

Upgrade path for existing cameras. ArcisAI's Bridge Device allows existing analog or older IP cameras to connect to the AI analytics and cloud VMS platform without full replacement, protecting the society's prior investment.

Privacy and resident consent. Face recognition in a residential setting must follow applicable data protection norms with clear resident communication. RWA committees should document their surveillance policy before enabling face-aware features.

Why Does Every Retail Store Need Smarter Surveillance Today?

Retail theft and shrinkage are among the most persistent cost pressures for Indian shop owners, whether you run a standalone kirana, a fashion outlet, or a multi-city supermarket chain. Industry estimates consistently place shrinkage — covering shoplifting, internal theft, vendor fraud, and administrative errors — at 1–3% of annual revenue. For a store turning over ₹1 crore a year, that is ₹1–3 lakh walking out the door.

Traditional CCTV records what happened. AI CCTV acts on what is happening. That shift — from passive recording to active intelligence — is what makes modern shop security cameras genuinely valuable for retail operators.
How Does AI CCTV Reduce Shoplifting in a Retail Store?
Shoplifting thrives on inattention — busy staff, crowded aisles, poorly lit corners. AI surveillance closes those gaps automatically.
Modern edge AI cameras process video directly on the device, without sending every frame to the cloud. This means instant, on-device detection of:
• Intrusion detection — alerts when someone enters a restricted area (stockroom, cash counter zone) without authorisation.
• Line-crossing alerts — triggers a notification the moment a defined boundary is crossed, even during peak shopping hours.
• Loitering and crowd detection — flags individuals who linger near high-value display areas longer than expected, giving staff time to engage proactively.
• Abandoned and missing object detection — identifies when a product is removed from a shelf and not taken to the billing counter, or when a bag is left unattended.
Because these detections happen at the camera level, alerts reach the store manager's mobile app in seconds — not after reviewing recordings the next morning.

Maharashtra consistently ranks among India's highest-investment states for urban infrastructure. Mumbai's scale — one of the world's most densely populated metros — makes city-wide surveillance both a significant operational challenge and an immediate public-safety priority.

Traditional CCTV in public spaces records events for review after they occur. AI surveillance transforms those cameras into proactive assets: systems that detect, classify, and alert in real time — without requiring a human operator to watch every feed simultaneously.

• Weapon detection: Alerts city-control operators when cameras detect objects associated with potential security threats in sensitive public locations.
• Intrusion detection: Perimeter protection for government buildings, infrastructure assets, substations, and restricted zones.

content.title: AI CCTV for Surat's Textile & Diamond Industry: Protecting High-Value Assets (2026)

children.text: Surat's diamond cutting and polishing units and its vast textile and saree manufacturing clusters face a shared security challenge: enormous concentrations of high-value, portable assets — loose diamonds, gemstones, premium fabrics — moving across busy production floors, shared corridors, and multi-unit trading buildings every day. AI-powered CCTV addresses this with real-time intrusion alerts, zone-by-zone access monitoring, encrypted audit-trail footage, and multi-unit oversight from a single dashboard — giving Surat's business owners the protection their inventory demands without disrupting the speed their industry runs on.
Why Does Surat's Diamond and Textile Industry Need Intelligent Surveillance?

Surat occupies a unique position in Indian and global trade. The city cuts and polishes more than 90 percent of the world's diamonds — operations concentrated in Varachha and Katargam, where thousands of small and mid-sized units handle loose stones worth lakhs to crores of rupees daily. Alongside this, Surat's Pandesara and Udhna belt is home to one of India's largest textile and synthetic saree manufacturing clusters, where high-value fabric inventory, embroidery stock, and finished goods move through mills, godowns, and trading complexes in large volumes.
The security risk profile these industries share is distinct from a generic factory or warehouse. The assets are:
• Small and concealable — a handful of polished diamonds or a bolt of premium fabric can leave a premises in a pocket or bag.
• High in unit value — a single incident of pilferage or theft can mean a loss that dwarfs months of operating profit.
• Handled by large workforces — production floors in both industries involve dozens to hundreds of workers in close proximity to high-value stock.
• Spread across multiple units — many Surat businesses operate from several floors of a shared building or across multiple locations in the same industrial cluster.

A conventional CCTV system — cameras that record passively and require manual review after an incident — does not match this risk environment. By the time footage is reviewed, the loss has already occurred. What Surat's diamond and textile businesses need is surveillance that detects, alerts, and creates a verifiable record in real time.
What Security Challenges Do Diamond and Textile Units in Surat Face?
How Can AI CCTV Protect Against Pilferage of Small, High-Value Assets?

In a diamond cutting or polishing unit, the primary internal theft risk is the removal of small stones — individually or incrementally over time. In a textile unit, it is the removal of premium fabric rolls, zari thread, or finished sarees. Both risks share a common characteristic: the items are small enough that a conventional perimeter camera cannot detect the theft event itself, only the person who may have committed it.
AI surveillance addresses this through a combination of capabilities:

• Missing object detection — cameras monitor designated storage areas, sorting tables, or inventory racks for the disappearance of specific objects or stacks. When an item that was present is no longer visible, the system flags the change and logs a timestamped alert — before anyone has reviewed footage manually.

• Zone access monitoring with intrusion alerts — restricted areas (vault rooms, finished-goods storage, diamond grading rooms) are configured with virtual perimeters. The moment an unauthorised person enters, an instant alert reaches the supervisor's phone via the mobile app.

• Line-crossing alerts — doorways, stairwells, and corridor checkpoints can be configured as virtual lines. Anyone crossing in a restricted direction or at an unauthorised time generates an automatic alert.
These detections run on the camera itself through edge AI — no cloud connection required for the alert to fire, and no delay from video travelling to a remote server and back.
How Can CCTV Help Manage Worker Zones and Access Control in Production Areas?

Both diamond and textile production involve highly specialised zones — grading rooms, polishing sections, finishing departments, raw material stores — where only specific workers should be present at specific times. Managing this manually across a multi-floor or multi-unit operation is extremely difficult.
AI surveillance supports zone management with:

• Face recognition at entry points (where lawfully deployed) — cameras at restricted zone entrances verify that the person attempting entry is authorised, generating access logs with timestamps automatically. This creates an audit trail showing exactly who was present in each zone at any given time — invaluable for incident investigations.
• Human detection with role-specific alerts — the system can be configured to alert when a person is detected in an area they should not occupy during a particular shift or time window.

• People counting analytics — headcount monitoring at production zone entries tracks how many personnel are present in each area at any moment, supporting both access control and occupancy management.
What Is the Risk at Gates and Entry Points for Surat Industrial Units?

Diamond units and textile mills typically operate within shared industrial estates or multi-tenant buildings where vehicle and pedestrian access is not always tightly controlled. Delivery vehicles, contractors, visitors, and casual labour may all access a facility on any given day. Without automated gate monitoring, it is difficult to maintain a reliable record of who entered and when.

ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition) cameras at vehicle entry points read and log every arriving and departing vehicle's number plate automatically. The system matches plates against an authorised or flagged list and alerts security staff to any unrecognised or blacklisted vehicle — creating a complete, searchable vehicle access log without manual effort.
For pedestrian entry, face recognition at access points creates an equivalent log for personnel.

content.title: BIS-ER Certification Explained: What It Means for CCTV Buyers (2026)

children.text: From 1 April 2026, every CCTV camera and IP recorder sold in India must carry a BIS-ER (Bureau of Indian Standards — Essential Requirements) certificate under the ER-01:2024 standard. This mandatory registration enforces six security baselines — from encrypted video to secure boot — that protect homes, businesses, and public infrastructure from cyber intrusion. Buyers who choose a BIS-ER certified CCTV camera get a device independently verified to meet India's national cybersecurity baseline.
What Is BIS-ER Certification for CCTV Cameras?

BIS-ER stands for Bureau of Indian Standards — Essential Requirements. It is a mandatory product-registration framework notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) through a gazette notification in April 2024, under the standard ER-01:2024.

Unlike voluntary quality marks, BIS-ER registration is a legal prerequisite for manufacturing, importing, or selling CCTV cameras, IP cameras, and network video recorders (NVRs/DVRs) in India. Products that do not carry a valid BIS-ER certificate cannot legally be placed on the Indian market from 1 April 2026 onward.

Testing is carried out at BIS-empanelled Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification (STQC) laboratories — 14 recognised labs across India — ensuring that assessments are independent and technically rigorous.
What Are the Six Essential Requirements?
The ER-01:2024 standard mandates six specific security controls. Every BIS-ER certified CCTV camera must comply with all six:
# — Requirement — What It Means for You
1 — No default passwords — Each device ships with a unique credential or forces a password change on first use — preventing mass credential-stuffing attacks.
2 — Encrypted video transmission — Video streams must use TLS/HTTPS, so footage cannot be intercepted in transit on your network or the internet.
3 — Secure signed-firmware boot — The camera only runs firmware that is cryptographically signed by the manufacturer, blocking malicious firmware injection.
4 — Disabled debug/test ports — Diagnostic interfaces (UART, JTAG, etc.) that attackers exploit for physical access must be disabled in production units.
5 — Supply-chain and chipset origin transparency — Manufacturers must disclose component sourcing, enabling buyers and regulators to assess geopolitical or supply-chain risk.
6 — Published vulnerability-disclosure policy — Brands must maintain a formal channel for security researchers to report flaws, with a committed remediation timeline.

These six controls directly address the most common attack vectors used against IoT surveillance devices — from botnet recruitment (Requirements 1 & 3) to passive eavesdropping (Requirement 2) and physical exploitation (Requirement 4).
BIS-ER vs. STQC Certification: What Is the Difference?
Both certifications come from the same government ecosystem, but they are not the same thing. Understanding the distinction is important — especially for enterprise, government, and PSU buyers.
Dimension — BIS-ER Registration — STQC Certification
Full name — BIS Essential Requirements (ER-01:2024) — Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification
Governed by — Bureau of Indian Standards / MeitY — STQC Directorate, MeitY
Scope — Hardware product (camera, recorder) — Software / system (VMS, platform, application)
Mandatory for — All CCTV products sold in India from 1 Apr 2026 — Government / PSU procurement; increasingly required in enterprise tenders
Audit depth — Lab testing of physical device against ER-01 — Deeper process and source-code-level security audit
Certificate visibility — crsbis.in / lims.bis.gov.in — stqc.gov.in
Who holds it — Manufacturer / importer — Software product owner

A brand offering both BIS-ER certified hardware and STQC-certified Video Management Software (VMS) provides end-to-end assurance — hardware security from the chip to the stream, and software security from the platform to the operator interface. That dual-layer posture is what government tenders and security-conscious enterprises are beginning to specify explicitly.
How to Verify a BIS-ER Certificate: Step-by-Step
Certification claims are only as valuable as your ability to independently verify them. Here is how to check any brand's BIS-ER status before you buy or specify.
Step 1 — Locate the Certificate Number

Ask the manufacturer or dealer for the BIS-ER registration certificate number. It follows the format R-XXXXXXXX ER01:2024. Reputable brands publish this on their website, product data sheets, and packaging.
Step 2 — Visit the Official BIS Portal
Go to crsbis.in (Compulsory Registration Scheme) or lims.bis.gov.in. These are the only authoritative sources maintained by the Bureau of Indian Standards.
Step 3 — Search by Certificate Number or Brand

Enter the certificate number or the applicant company name in the search field. The portal will return the registered product models, certificate validity dates, and the testing lab that performed the assessment.
Step 4 — Cross-Check the Product Model

Confirm that the specific model you are purchasing is listed under the certificate — not just the brand. Certificates are issued per model or model family; a certified flagship does not automatically cover a lower-end SKU.
Step 5 — Verify STQC Certification Separately (for Software)
For VMS or platform software, visit stqc.gov.in and search the certified products directory. If a vendor claims STQC-certified software, the certificate should be publicly listed there.
Why BIS-ER Certification Matters to You as a Buyer
For Homeowners and Small Businesses

The six mandatory controls mean that a BIS-ER certified CCTV camera cannot be trivially commandeered into a botnet, cannot broadcast unencrypted footage over your network, and will receive security patches through a formal process. These are not marketing promises — they are verified, legally mandated baselines.
For IT Managers and Security Integrators

BIS-ER compliance reduces your regulatory exposure. If a non-certified device on your network is compromised and used in an attack, the liability question becomes difficult. Specifying certified hardware — and insisting on verified certificates before commissioning — is now standard due diligence.
For Government and PSU Project Managers

MeitY's mandate effectively aligns surveillance procurement with the broader Digital India security posture. For projects requiring STQC-certified VMS in addition to BIS-ER hardware, the dual-certification requirement narrows the qualified vendor list considerably. Verifying both certificates before finalising a bill of materials is no longer optional.
ArcisAI and BIS-ER: End-to-End Certified Surveillance

ArcisAI — the surveillance brand of Adiance Technologies (founded 2003, headquartered in Ahmedabad) — holds BIS-ER certificate R-72003735 ER01:2024 for its camera hardware, and its VMS platform carries STQC certification. This makes ArcisAI one of a small number of Indian brands offering the complete dual-certified stack: independently verified hardware security at the device level, and independently audited software security at the platform level.

Beyond certification, ArcisAI cameras are Made in India and NDAA compliant (meeting US National Defense Authorization Act supply-chain standards — a globally recognised benchmark for component origin transparency). On-camera edge AI processes up to eight concurrent detection types without sending raw video to the cloud, and the ArcisGPT interface allows operators to query video archives in natural language.

For buyers who need to demonstrate due diligence — whether to an insurer, a government auditor, or an enterprise board — the combination of BIS-ER registration, STQC VMS certification, NDAA compliance, and Made in India manufacturing provides a documented, multi-jurisdictional compliance trail.

The meaningful differentiator is the combination of BIS-ER certified hardware, STQC-certified VMS, and a manufacturer whose supply chain and AI capabilities are built for the Indian market from the ground up. > Editorial note: Certificate numbers, portal URLs, and regulatory dates cited in this article were accurate as of the publication date. content.title: How to Choose an AI CCTV Camera in India (2026 Checklist)

children.text: Quick answer: Choosing the best AI CCTV camera in India means matching resolution (3–8 MP), camera form factor, connectivity (PoE/WiFi/4G), edge or cloud AI capability, BIS-ER certified hardware, and STQC-certified VMS software to your site's specific needs — then verifying service coverage and total cost of ownership before you commit.
Why Does Choosing the Right AI CCTV Camera Matter?

India's surveillance market is growing fast, and so is the number of cameras claiming "AI" capability. Not every product delivers meaningful intelligence, reliable uptime, or compliance with Indian standards. A wrong purchase means wasted capital, recurring false alarms, and security gaps. This guide cuts through the noise with a practical, step-by-step framework any buyer can use — from a single shop to a multi-site enterprise.
What Certifications Should You Look For?
Certification is the single most important filter before you evaluate any other spec.
BIS-ER Certification for Hardware

The Bureau of Indian Standards Electronics and IT Goods (Mandatory Registration) Order requires surveillance cameras sold in India to carry a BIS-ER mark. This confirms the hardware meets Indian safety and electromagnetic compatibility standards and is manufactured or tested under a registered process. When evaluating a camera, ask the vendor for their BIS Registration Number and verify it on crsbis.in.
STQC Certification for VMS Software

This is the certification most buyers overlook — and it matters most for WiFi-connected and cloud-capable cameras. The Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification (STQC) Directorate under MeitY certifies Video Management Software (VMS) for security, reliability, and data-handling standards. A camera's hardware may be BIS-ER certified, but if the VMS or mobile app transmitting your video has not been STQC certified, your data security and compliance posture is unverified. Always ask for STQC certification on the VMS, not just the camera body. Verify on stqc.gov.in.
What Resolution Do You Actually Need?
Higher resolution is not always better — it comes at a cost in storage, bandwidth, and processing. Use this as a baseline:
Resolution — Pixels — Best For
3 MP — ~2048 × 1536 — General monitoring, corridors, small retail
5 MP — ~2592 × 1944 — Parking lots, mid-size offices, warehouses
8 MP (4K) — ~3840 × 2160 — Entry points, license plate reading, large open areas

For most Indian SME sites, 5 MP strikes the right balance between image clarity and storage economy. If you need to read number plates or identify individuals at distance, consider 8 MP at critical points and 3–5 MP elsewhere.
Which Camera Type Is Right for Your Location?
Camera form factor is a physical and functional decision. The table below maps each type to its ideal deployment scenario.
Camera Type — Typical Coverage — Best Use Cases — Key Limitation
Bullet — Narrow, long-distance — Perimeter, parking lanes, entry gates — Fixed angle; visible deterrent
Dome — Wide, 180° — Retail floors, lobbies, ceilings — Shorter range than bullet
PTZ — 360° pan/tilt/optical zoom — Large open spaces, stadiums, campuses — Higher cost; moving parts
Mini-PTZ — Compact 360°/zoom — Meeting rooms, mid-size retail, restaurants — Lower zoom range than full PTZ
Covert/Cube — Discreet — Offices, reception desks — Not for outdoor or wide-area
A layered approach — bullet cameras on perimeter walls, domes on ceilings indoors, one PTZ per large open zone — typically gives the best coverage-to-cost ratio.
What Connectivity Option Should You Choose: PoE, WiFi, or 4G?

Power over Ethernet (PoE) is the most reliable choice for permanent installations. A single Cat-6 cable carries both power and data, eliminating separate power cabling and reducing failure points. PoE cameras are recommended for warehouses, manufacturing plants, and any site where cabling is feasible.

WiFi cameras are faster to deploy and cost-effective for small retail or rented premises. Their trade-off: susceptibility to interference, network congestion, and the added importance of a STQC-certified VMS (since all video travels over your wireless network).

4G/LTE cameras suit remote sites — construction zones, agricultural land, or highway installations — where wired and WiFi infrastructure is absent. Factor in recurring SIM/data costs in your TCO calculation.
What Is the Difference Between Edge AI and Cloud AI?
This distinction determines where the intelligence lives and directly affects latency, bandwidth, privacy, and scalability.
Edge AI (On-Camera Processing)

Edge AI cameras embed an AI chip (typically an NPU or DSP) directly in the camera. Detections — such as person, vehicle, intrusion, loitering, crowd density, or face recognition — happen on the device itself, in milliseconds, without sending raw video to a server.
Advantages: Low latency, works during network outages, preserves bandwidth, keeps raw video local (strong for privacy-sensitive sites).
Best for: Retail stores, banks, residential complexes, sites with limited bandwidth.
Cloud AI (Server-Side Analytics)
Cloud AI sends video streams to a central server or cloud platform, where more powerful computing runs analytics — typically at larger scale, across many cameras simultaneously.
Advantages: Unlimited processing power, scalable to hundreds of cameras, enables cross-camera correlation and city-scale analytics.
Best for: Large enterprises, smart city deployments, multi-site operators who need aggregated insights.
Hybrid approach: Many modern deployments use edge AI for real-time on-site alerts and cloud AI for retrospective analytics, reporting, and multi-site dashboards — giving you the best of both.
Does Night Vision Technology Matter?
Yes. Two technologies dominate:

Infrared (IR) Night Vision illuminates the scene invisibly and renders video in black and white. It works at long ranges (up to 50–80 m on quality cameras) and consumes less power. Suitable for perimeters and parking areas.

Color Night Vision (Full-Color) uses a large image sensor and supplemental white-light LEDs to produce color images in low light. Color footage makes identification — clothing color, vehicle color — significantly easier. Better for entrances and indoor areas where color detail aids incident review.
For critical entry points, color night vision is worth the modest premium.
What Weatherproofing Rating Do You Need?
IP66 — Dust-tight and protected against powerful water jets. Suitable for most Indian outdoor environments including monsoon conditions.
IP67 — Dust-tight and can withstand temporary immersion up to 1 m. Required for flood-prone ground-level installations or industrial wash-down environments.
For rooftop and outdoor perimeter cameras in India, IP66 is the minimum acceptable standard.
How Should You Think About Storage?
Storage strategy has a direct impact on ongoing costs and footage accessibility.
• SD Card (on-camera): Lowest cost, good for single-camera or small sites. Vulnerable to tampering if the camera is physically accessible.
• NVR (Network Video Recorder): Centralized, secure on-premises storage. Recommended for 4+ cameras. Choose NVRs with RAID or redundancy for critical sites.
• Cloud Storage: Enables remote access and off-site backup. Factor in ongoing subscription cost. Ensure your cloud provider and VMS are compliant with Indian data residency requirements.
A practical rule: retain 15–30 days of footage for most commercial sites, and 60–90 days for finance, healthcare, or government sites.
What Should You Evaluate in the VMS and Mobile App?
The VMS (Video Management Software) is the brain of your camera system. Evaluate it as rigorously as the camera hardware:
• Live view and multi-camera grid: Can operators monitor all cameras from one screen?
• Search and playback: Can you search footage by event type (motion, intrusion, face) rather than scrubbing through hours of video?
• Alert management: Are AI alerts actionable and configurable? Can you set schedules and sensitivity zones?
• Mobile app: Does it support live view, playback, and push notifications on both Android and iOS?
• STQC Certification: As noted above, this is the quality and security benchmark for VMS software sold in India.
Is Scalability and Multi-Site Management Important?

If you operate more than one site — or plan to grow — choose a platform that supports multi-site management from a single dashboard. This means centralized health monitoring, unified alert feeds, consolidated reporting, and role-based access so branch managers see only their own cameras. Buying a single-site-only system and expanding later often results in fragmented infrastructure and higher long-term cost.
What About Service, Warranty, and Support?
Hardware quality is irrelevant if support is unavailable. Before purchasing, confirm:
• Warranty period: Minimum 1 year; 3 years is better for infrastructure cameras.
• On-site service coverage: Does the vendor or their partner have engineers in your city or district?
• SLA for camera replacement or repair: 24–48 hours is a reasonable benchmark for commercial installations.
• Firmware update policy: AI cameras should receive regular firmware and model updates to stay effective.
Does Made-in-India or NDAA Compliance Matter for Your Use Case?

For government tenders and PSU projects, Made-in-India cameras manufactured under MEITY/MHA guidelines or PLI schemes receive preference in procurement. Always verify with your specific tender requirements.

For export projects or any deployment involving US government-funded infrastructure, cameras must be NDAA (National Defense Authorization Act) compliant — meaning they cannot contain components from certain restricted manufacturers. NDAA compliance is increasingly requested in enterprise and hospitality procurement as well, even outside government contexts.
What Is Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)?
The purchase price of a camera is typically 40–60% of its true 3-year cost. Factor in:
Cost Component — Notes
Camera hardware — One-time
NVR / storage — One-time + expansion
Cabling & installation — One-time
VMS license — Annual or per-camera
Cloud storage subscription — Monthly/annual
4G/SIM data costs — Monthly (if applicable)
Maintenance & support — Annual contract
Firmware/AI model updates — Included or paid?
Always ask vendors for a 3-year TCO estimate, not just the hardware sticker price.
The 10-Point AI CCTV Buying Checklist
Use this before signing any purchase order:
1. BIS-ER hardware certification confirmed — verify the registration number on crsbis.in
2. STQC-certified VMS software confirmed — verify on stqc.gov.in (critical for WiFi/cloud cameras)
3. Resolution matched to use case — 3 MP / 5 MP / 8 MP selected per camera location
4. Camera type selected per zone — bullet/dome/PTZ/mini-PTZ mapped to site plan
5. Connectivity method chosen — PoE for permanent, WiFi for flexible, 4G for remote
6. Edge AI or cloud AI capability confirmed — and deployment model chosen
7. Night vision type selected — IR for perimeter/distance, color for entry/ID purposes
8. IP66 or IP67 weatherproofing confirmed for all outdoor cameras
9. Storage plan and retention period defined — SD / NVR / cloud / hybrid
10. Service SLA, warranty, and multi-site scalability confirmed with vendor in writing
Where Does ArcisAI Fit?
For buyers who want a single vendor covering all the boxes above, ArcisAI (arcisai.io) — by Adiance Technologies, founded in 2003 — is a strong Indian option worth evaluating:
• BIS-ER certified hardware: Registration No. R-72003735 under ER01:2024 (verify on crsbis.in)
• STQC-certified VMS: Software certified by STQC Directorate, MeitY
• Edge AI: Eight on-camera detections including intrusion, loitering, crowd density, and more — processing on the device, not the cloud
• ArcisGPT: A conversational AI interface that lets operators query camera footage in natural language
• Bridge Device: A retrofit solution that adds AI intelligence to existing non-AI cameras, protecting legacy infrastructure investment
• Made in India and NDAA compliant: Suitable for government tenders, PSU deployments, and export projects
• Enterprise scalability: Multi-site management for large and distributed deployments
ArcisAI is one strong option among several in the market. The checklist above applies regardless of which vendor you choose.

content.title: How to Evaluate an AI CCTV Brand in India (2026)

children.text: Quick answer: To choose the best AI CCTV camera brand in India, evaluate vendors across ten dimensions: BIS-ER hardware certification plus STQC-certified VMS software, edge AI capability, Made-in-India and NDAA compliance, ecosystem completeness, retrofit options, manufacturing heritage, support network, multi-site scalability, data-hosting controls, and total cost of ownership. Use the scoring checklist below to rank any brand objectively.
Why Does Brand Selection Matter More Than Individual Camera Specs?

Buying a single camera is straightforward. Deploying surveillance across a factory campus, a retail chain, or a government facility is a different challenge entirely. A great camera paired with a poor Video Management System (VMS), absent local service, or unverified certifications can leave you with an expensive liability instead of a security asset.

Brand evaluation shifts the question from "which camera has the best spec sheet?" to "which company can I trust to keep my sites secure, compliant, and supported over the next five years?" That framing leads to far better purchasing decisions.
This framework is vendor-neutral: ten measurable criteria and a scoring checklist you can apply to any brand you are considering.
What Are the Ten Criteria for Evaluating an AI CCTV Brand?
1. Certification Depth — Does the Brand Cover Hardware AND Software?
The most commonly overlooked distinction in the Indian market is that BIS-ER and STQC are two separate certifications covering two different layers of your system.

BIS-ER (Bureau of Indian Standards — Electronics & IT Goods Mandatory Registration) covers the physical camera hardware: safety, electromagnetic compatibility, and manufacturing standards. You can verify any BIS registration number on crsbis.in.

STQC (Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification) covers VMS software: security testing, source-code review, and data-handling practices. For WiFi and cloud-connected cameras — where the software layer controls remote access, live streaming credentials, and cloud data routing — STQC certification on the VMS is especially critical. An uncertified VMS is the attack surface no spec sheet will warn you about. Verify STQC certifications at stqc.gov.in.
A brand that holds only BIS-ER (hardware) but not STQC (VMS) has a gap at exactly the point where modern threats are most likely to enter.
What "good" looks like: Both BIS-ER registration (with a verifiable registration number) and STQC certification for the VMS, independently verified on government portals.
2. AI Capability — Edge vs. Cloud, and Which Detections Actually Matter?
"AI camera" is one of the most overused phrases in surveillance marketing. Probe deeper with two questions:

• Where does the AI run? Edge AI processes video on the camera's own processor — detections happen in milliseconds, work during network outages, and avoid sending raw video to a server. Cloud AI depends on a continuous upload link and introduces latency. For most deployments, edge AI is the more resilient architecture.

• Which detections are useful for your use case? A camera that does motion detection is not meaningfully "AI." Look for object classification (person, vehicle, package), intrusion detection, loitering alerts, crowd density, fire/smoke detection, and behavioural analytics relevant to your sector.

What "good" looks like: Documented edge-AI detections with at least five to eight specific use cases listed, clear disclosure of which analytics run on-device vs. in the cloud, and a roadmap for new capabilities.
3. Made-in-India and NDAA Compliance — Why Does Origin Matter?
For government projects, PSUs, defence-adjacent facilities, and export-facing organisations, two compliance dimensions are non-negotiable:

• Made in India / ALMM: Products qualifying under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers get preference in government tenders. Genuine domestic manufacturing — not just assembly — signals a stable, auditable supply chain.

• NDAA Section 889 compliance: US law prohibits federal procurement of surveillance equipment from certain manufacturers. Indian firms working with US-headquartered clients or selling into US markets increasingly face this requirement in supply-chain audits. A NDAA-compliant brand avoids those procurement blockers before they arise.
What "good" looks like: Documented domestic manufacturing (not just "assembled in India"), a PLI or ALMM listing where applicable, and an explicit NDAA-compliance statement from the vendor.
4. Ecosystem Completeness — Cameras Alone Are Not a Solution

A reliable AI surveillance deployment requires every layer to interoperate cleanly: cameras, NVR/DVR hardware, VMS software, analytics engine, and — increasingly — a GenAI layer for natural-language querying of footage and events. When these components come from different vendors, integration complexity, finger-pointing during outages, and firmware incompatibilities multiply.

What "good" looks like: One vendor offering cameras, NVR, VMS, and analytics under a single support contract, with a documented API for third-party integrations and a GenAI layer for operator-facing intelligence.
5. Retrofit and Upgrade Path — Can the Brand Work With What You Already Have?

Ripping out existing infrastructure to adopt a new platform has a cost that rarely appears in the initial quote. Brands that offer bridge devices — hardware or software adapters that bring older analog or third-party IP cameras into the same AI management platform — dramatically reduce deployment cost and disruption for established sites.
What "good" looks like: A documented retrofit device or adapter, compatibility listed for major third-party camera brands, and a phased upgrade programme rather than a forced full replacement.
6. Manufacturing Heritage and R&D — How Long Has the Brand Been at This?

Surveillance is a long-cycle investment. A brand founded last year around a rebranded off-the-shelf camera module carries a different risk profile from one with decades of R&D, filed patents, and engineering staff focused on product development.

What "good" looks like: Five-plus years of documented surveillance product history, in-house hardware and software R&D, and evidence of ongoing investment (new models, firmware updates, filed patents).
7. Service, Warranty, and Support Network — Who Comes When Something Breaks?

A camera that fails in the middle of the night on a remote site is only as good as the service response behind it. Evaluate the actual support network: number of authorised service centres, response-time SLAs, on-site vs. depot repair, warranty duration, and whether the local dealer is trained or simply a reseller.
What "good" looks like: Minimum three-year warranty, pan-India authorised service network with documented SLAs, dedicated technical support, and clear escalation paths for enterprise accounts.
8. Scalability and Multi-Site Management — Does It Grow With You?

A system that works beautifully for a single 32-camera site may collapse under the management overhead of a 50-site retail chain. Evaluate the VMS architecture for centralised multi-site dashboards, role-based access control, remote health monitoring, and bandwidth-efficient video retrieval.

What "good" looks like: Multi-site deployment references, a VMS that supports hundreds of cameras without linear hardware scaling, and built-in tools for remote firmware updates and health monitoring.
9. Data Hosting and Privacy Controls — Where Does Your Footage Actually Live?

This criterion has grown sharply in importance as cloud-connected cameras proliferate. Key questions: Does footage leave India? Who holds the encryption keys — you or the vendor? What is the data-retention and deletion policy? Is the cloud infrastructure on Indian servers compliant with the applicable data-protection framework?

What "good" looks like: India-domiciled storage (or on-premises options), customer-controlled encryption keys, documented retention and deletion policies, and controls aligned with India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
10. Total Cost of Ownership — Looking Beyond the Camera Price Tag

The camera price is typically a small fraction of five-year system cost. Factor in: VMS licensing (per-camera or per-site), annual maintenance contracts, storage (local NVR vs. cloud), and upgrade pricing for new AI features.
What "good" looks like: Published, predictable licensing; all-inclusive AMC option; storage cost reference; and a clear policy for feature updates (included vs. paid).
Evaluation Criteria Summary Table
# — Criterion — What "Good" Looks Like — Red Flags
1 — Certification depth — BIS-ER + STQC (both verifiable on govt portals) — Hardware cert only; no STQC on VMS
2 — AI capability — 5–8+ edge detections; documented on-device vs. cloud split — "AI-ready" with no specifics
3 — Made-in-India + NDAA — Domestic manufacturing, ALMM/PLI listed, NDAA statement — "Assembled in India" with imported modules only
4 — Ecosystem completeness — Cameras + NVR + VMS + analytics + GenAI under one roof — Camera-only brand with OEM VMS
5 — Retrofit/upgrade path — Bridge device for legacy cameras; phased upgrade plan — Forced full replacement required
6 — Manufacturing heritage — 5+ years R&D, in-house hardware and software teams — Founded post-2022 with rebranded hardware
7 — Service & warranty — 3-year warranty; pan-India service network with SLAs — 1-year warranty; depot repair only
8 — Scalability — Multi-site VMS, centralised dashboard, remote health monitoring — Single-site VMS without enterprise tier
9 — Data hosting & privacy — India-domiciled storage; customer-controlled encryption — Footage routed overseas by default
10 — Total cost of ownership — Transparent licensing; predictable AMC; storage calculator — Hidden per-camera cloud fees
How Do You Score a Brand? (Printable Checklist)
Use this 10-point checklist. Each criterion is scored 0, 1, or 2:
• 2 = Fully meets the "good" standard with verifiable evidence
• 1 = Partially meets the standard or documentation is incomplete
• 0 = Does not meet the standard or information is unavailable
# — Criterion — Score (0–2) — Notes
1 — BIS-ER registration verified on crsbis.in + STQC VMS cert verified on stqc.gov.in —  —
2 — Edge AI with 5+ documented detection types, on-device processing confirmed —  —
3 — Domestic manufacturing confirmed; NDAA compliance statement provided —  —
4 — Full ecosystem: cameras + NVR + VMS + analytics + GenAI from one vendor —  —
5 — Retrofit/bridge device available for legacy cameras —  —
6 — 5+ years product history; in-house R&D team documented —  —
7 — 3-year warranty + pan-India authorised service network + SLA provided —  —
8 — Multi-site VMS with centralised dashboard; 100+ camera references —  —
9 — India-domiciled storage; customer-controlled keys; DPDP-aligned policy —  —
10 — All-inclusive licensing published; five-year TCO estimate available —  —
— TOTAL — /20 —

Interpretation: 17–20: mature vendor, proceed to proof-of-concept. 12–16: credible but seek written commitments on gaps before contracting. 8–11: significant gaps, request a compliance roadmap and independent references. Below 8: high-risk selection, evaluate alternatives first.
Where Does ArcisAI Stand Against These Criteria?
To illustrate how the framework applies in practice, here is how ArcisAI (by Adiance Technologies, founded 2003) scores on each criterion:
1. Certifications: BIS-ER certified hardware (Registration No. R-72003735, ER01:2024, verifiable on crsbis.in) and STQC-certified VMS (verifiable on stqc.gov.in) — end-to-end coverage.
2. AI capability: Eight edge-AI detections on-device, plus ArcisGPT — a GenAI layer for natural-language footage querying.
3. Made-in-India + NDAA: Manufactured in India by Adiance Technologies; NDAA-compliant.
4. Ecosystem: Cameras, NVR, VMS, analytics, and ArcisGPT developed under one brand.
5. Retrofit: Bridge Device available to bring third-party cameras into the ArcisAI platform.
6. Heritage: Adiance Technologies has operated since 2003 with in-house hardware and software R&D.
7. Service: Pan-India support network; consult arcisai.io for current warranty and SLA terms.
8. Scalability: Multi-site VMS architecture; consult arcisai.io for enterprise deployment references.
9. Data hosting: India-domiciled infrastructure; consult arcisai.io for current DPDP alignment documentation.
10. TCO: Consult arcisai.io for current licensing and AMC pricing.
ArcisAI is one example of a brand that meets these criteria. Apply the same checklist to every vendor you evaluate.

content.title: India's 2026 CCTV Security Rules (BIS-ER & STQC): A Buyer's Guide

children.text: From 1 April 2026, every CCTV camera sold in India must carry STQC certification under the Bureau of Indian Standards Essential Requirements framework (ER-01:2024). This security mandate — issued by MeitY in April 2024 and phased in over two years — sets six mandatory cybersecurity baselines that any manufacturer, domestic or foreign, must meet before selling new units in India. Understanding these requirements is now essential for any buyer, integrator, or procurement team specifying surveillance equipment.
What Changed on 1 April 2026?

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) published its gazette notification in April 2024, giving the industry two years to comply. From 1 April 2026, every CCTV camera sold in India must be certified under the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Essential Requirements framework — specifically ER-01:2024 — and must carry a valid STQC (Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification) approval.

This is not a product ban in the traditional sense. It is a security certification mandate — similar to how electronics must carry BIS marks before they can be sold legally in India. Cameras already installed continue to operate. The rule governs new procurement only.
Why Did the Government Act Now?

The mandate responds to long-standing concerns about the cybersecurity posture of surveillance hardware. Globally, procurement regulators across the United States (NDAA 2019), the United Kingdom, Australia, and several EU member states have tightened controls on surveillance equipment — primarily over data-security and supply-chain transparency concerns.

India's approach is technology-neutral: rather than naming specific brands, MeitY set technical security baselines that any manufacturer must meet. The practical effect is clear: brands that did not invest in the certification process in time are unable to legally sell new units under the new framework.
The Six Essential Requirements Every CCTV Must Meet
The BIS ER-01:2024 framework specifies six mandatory security requirements. Any CCTV camera sold in India after 1 April 2026 must satisfy all six.
# — Essential Requirement — What It Means in Practice
1 — No default passwords — Devices must force unique credentials on first setup
2 — Encrypted video transmission — TLS/HTTPS required for all video streams
3 — Secure signed-firmware boot — Only cryptographically verified firmware may run
4 — Disabled debug ports — Physical debug interfaces (UART/JTAG) must be locked
5 — Supply-chain/chipset origin transparency — Manufacturers must disclose component origins
6 — Published vulnerability-disclosure policy — A formal CVD process must be documented and accessible

These requirements are not theoretical — they address real attack vectors. Default credentials and unencrypted streams are the two most commonly exploited entry points in IP camera breaches. Unsigned firmware enables persistent malware. Disabled debug ports prevent on-device tampering after deployment.
Before vs. After April 2026: What Actually Changed
Dimension — Before 1 April 2026 — After 1 April 2026
Non-certified camera new sales — Permitted — Not legally permitted without STQC cert
Existing installed cameras — Operational — Continue to operate (rule is not retroactive)
Government procurement — Largely uncertified — STQC certification mandatory
Indian brand market share — ~33% — 80%+ (post-mandate estimate)
Certification verification — No central check — Verify at crsbis.in / stqc.gov.in
Are Existing Cameras Affected?

No. The mandate is prospective, not retroactive. Cameras that were purchased and installed before 1 April 2026 may continue to operate legally. Organizations are not required to replace existing infrastructure.
However, organizations running older, uncertified hardware should consider two practical points:
1. Security posture: Cameras lacking the six ER-01:2024 controls are more exposed to the attack classes those controls address.
2. Future procurement: When expanding or replacing cameras, new purchases must be STQC-certified, which may create a mixed-estate management consideration.
Who Is Most Affected?
Government and PSU Buyers

New procurement rules for central and state government, defence, and public sector undertakings require STQC-certified hardware. Non-certified cameras cannot be specified in new tenders from April 2026 onwards.
Private Enterprises and Residential Projects

Technically, the BIS mandate applies to all sales in India, not just government. A retailer selling uncertified stock after the deadline is non-compliant. Channel partners and importers who did not transition to certified product pipelines before the cut-off face legal exposure.
System Integrators
Integrators who specify or install non-certified cameras on new projects after the deadline carry compliance risk, particularly on government, banking, or critical-infrastructure contracts.
What Does "CCTV Brands That Have Not Completed STQC Certification" Mean for Buyers?

The certification requirement is brand-agnostic. Several major imported camera brands — including some that previously held large market share in India — did not complete STQC certification under ER-01:2024, and new units of their CCTV products therefore cannot be legally sold in India from April 2026. The market shift from roughly one-third domestic share to over 80% reflects the scale of this transition. Buyers should verify any brand's current certification status on the official portals before purchasing.
Certified Alternatives: What to Look For

Buyers who need STQC-compliant cameras have a growing list of certified options. Before purchasing, verify any claimed certification number on the official portals: crsbis.in (BIS) or stqc.gov.in (STQC).
ArcisAI

ArcisAI is an Indian AI-first surveillance brand building hardware and software certified under the new framework. Their cameras carry BIS-ER certification (reference: R-72003735 ER01:2024) and their Video Management System (VMS) holds STQC certification. The platform is NDAA compliant and Made in India. Key differentiators include edge AI with eight onboard detection types and ArcisGPT, a natural-language interface for searching and querying footage. For organisations moving to a fully certified, AI-capable stack, ArcisAI offers certified hardware, certified VMS, and integrated analytics — without reliance on overseas chipsets or external cloud infrastructure.
Other Certified Indian Brands
• CP Plus — The largest Indian CCTV brand by volume; wide product range across segments.
• Prama — Indian manufacturer with a focus on HD and IP cameras.
• Matrix — Pune-based brand strong in enterprise and access-control integration.
• Sparsh — Domestic manufacturer serving both commercial and government verticals.
• HiFocus — Chennai-based brand with an established government supply track record.
Always request the BIS-ER or STQC certificate number from your vendor and cross-check it on the official portals before committing to a purchase or specification.
How to Verify a CCTV's STQC Certification
1. Ask your vendor for the BIS Registration Number or STQC Test Certificate number.
2. Visit crsbis.in and search by registration number or product category.
3. Confirm the certificate is valid (not expired), covers the specific model, and references ER-01:2024.
4. Optionally cross-check at stqc.gov.in for STQC-specific test reports.
If a vendor cannot provide a verifiable certificate number, treat that as a red flag.

content.title: What is STQC Certification for CCTV? (2026 Buyer's Guide)

children.text: STQC (Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification) certification for CCTV is a mandatory security compliance programme run by India's MeitY. From 1 April 2026, CCTV systems sold in India must meet Essential Requirements (ER-01:2024) covering cybersecurity, encrypted video, and supply-chain transparency. STQC certification is specifically required for government and PSU procurement.
Why Does STQC Certification for CCTV Matter in 2026?

For years, India's surveillance market included a significant share of imported hardware where cybersecurity standards varied widely — cameras that shipped with factory-default passwords, unencrypted video streams, and chipsets of undisclosed origin. As city-wide and critical-infrastructure deployments grew, so did the risk: a single unpatched camera can become an entry point into a sensitive network.

In April 2024, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) published the Essential Requirements gazette notification ER-01:2024. Effective 1 April 2026, this framework has two enforcement pillars:
1. BIS-ER (Bureau of Indian Standards — Essential Requirements) — a product registration that hardware manufacturers must obtain before selling cameras in India.

2. STQC Certification — a deeper, lab-tested security audit run by Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification Directorate (under MeitY) that is compulsory for government and PSU procurement tenders.
Together, these two certifications form India's answer to the question: "Is this surveillance system safe enough to protect public infrastructure?"
What Are the Six Security Essentials Under ER-01:2024?
Any CCTV camera or Video Management System (VMS) targeting the Indian market — especially government projects — must satisfy all six Essential Requirements:
# — Requirement — What It Means in Practice
1 — No default passwords — Cameras must force a password change on first login; factory credentials cannot remain active
2 — Encrypted video transmission — All streams must use TLS/HTTPS; unencrypted RTSP to the open internet is not permitted
3 — Secure, signed-firmware boot — Firmware must be cryptographically signed; unsigned or tampered firmware must be rejected at boot
4 — Disabled debug/test ports — UART, JTAG, and other diagnostic ports must be physically or logically disabled in production units
5 — Supply-chain and chipset origin transparency — Manufacturers must disclose the origin of SoCs, modules, and critical components
6 — Published vulnerability-disclosure policy — A documented, public process for reporting and patching security flaws must exist
These requirements are technology-neutral — they apply equally to dome cameras, PTZ units, bullet cameras, NVRs, and VMS software platforms.
BIS-ER vs STQC: What Is the Difference?
This is the question buyers most frequently get wrong. The two certifications are complementary, not interchangeable.
Parameter — BIS-ER Registration — STQC Certification
Issuing body — Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) — STQC Directorate, MeitY
Scope — Hardware products (cameras, NVRs) — Hardware and/or software (VMS, platforms)
Testing depth — Document review + factory audit — Full lab-based security testing
Mandatory for — All CCTV sold commercially in India (from Apr 2026) — Government and PSU procurement specifically
Where to verify — crsbis.in / lims.bis.gov.in — stqc.gov.in
Covers ER-01:2024? — Yes — Yes (plus additional security layers)
Typical validity — 2 years (renewable) — Project/contract specific; check certificate date

Bottom line: A product can have BIS-ER without STQC, but for any government tender you need both. A product with STQC implicitly satisfies BIS-ER requirements, but you should still verify both certificates independently on the official portals.
Which CCTV Brands Are STQC Certified?
As of mid-2026, the publicly known brands on the STQC-certified camera list include:
• Prama
• CP Plus
• Sparsh
• Matrix
• Honeywell
• Vicon
• Equus

Several major imported camera brands that previously held large market share in India have not completed STQC certification and therefore cannot legally be sold as new products under the current regime. Domestic and India-compliant brands now account for approximately 80% or more of new camera sales — a significant market shift driven by early investment in cybersecurity compliance.
How to verify: Always cross-check any vendor's certificate claim directly on stqc.gov.in and crsbis.in or lims.bis.gov.in. Certificate numbers should be publicly searchable.
What About STQC Certified VMS Software?

Most buyers focus on camera hardware, but the ER-01:2024 framework also applies to Video Management System software — the platform that records, manages, and analyses camera feeds. A VMS that connects compliant cameras to a non-compliant backend can still introduce vulnerabilities.
STQC certification for VMS evaluates:
• Authentication and role-based access controls
• Encryption of stored video and metadata
• Audit logging and tamper detection
• Secure API endpoints
When procuring for government or critical infrastructure, request both the hardware BIS-ER certificate and the VMS STQC certificate from your vendor.
ArcisAI: An AI-First Example of Dual Compliance
For buyers evaluating modern, AI-capable systems, ArcisAI (by Adiance Technologies, Ahmedabad — parent company founded 2003) is one example of a vendor that holds both certifications:
• BIS-ER Certificate: R-72003735 (ER01:2024) — verifiable on crsbis.in / lims.bis.gov.in
• STQC Certification: For its VMS software platform — verifiable on stqc.gov.in

ArcisAI cameras are Made in India and NDAA compliant. The platform includes edge AI with up to eight on-camera detections (running inference locally, without sending raw video to external clouds) and ArcisGPT, a conversational AI interface for querying footage and alerts.

This dual-compliance approach — hardware BIS-ER plus software STQC — is the model that large government and smart-city deployments are increasingly requiring. ArcisAI is one option worth evaluating; buyers should request the certificate numbers, verify them on the official portals, and compare against other compliant vendors on the list.
How to Verify STQC and BIS-ER Certificates Yourself
Do not rely solely on vendor-supplied PDFs. Here is the three-step verification process:
1. Ask the vendor for their BIS-ER registration number and their STQC certificate number (or reference).
2. Check BIS-ER at crsbis.in or lims.bis.gov.in — search by registration number or brand name.
3. Check STQC at stqc.gov.in — navigate to the certified products/empanelled products section and search by vendor or product name.
If a certificate does not appear in the official database, it should be treated as unverified regardless of what documentation the vendor provides.
What Should Procurement Teams Ask Vendors?
If you are a government IT officer, PSU procurement manager, or systems integrator working on a tender, use this checklist:
• [ ] Provide BIS-ER registration number (hardware cameras/NVRs)
• [ ] Provide STQC certificate reference (VMS or camera software)
• [ ] Confirm chipset/SoC origin as disclosed in ER-01:2024 compliance documentation
• [ ] Provide signed-firmware update policy and release notes
• [ ] Share published vulnerability-disclosure policy URL
• [ ] Confirm debug ports are disabled (request test report)
• [ ] Confirm default passwords are blocked at firmware level
Any vendor unable to answer these questions in writing should be treated with caution in a government procurement context.

items.question: Is STQC certification the same as BIS certification?

children.text: No. BIS-ER is a product registration issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards covering hardware compliance with ER-01:2024. STQC certification is a lab-tested security audit issued by MeitY's STQC Directorate. Both are required for government procurement; BIS-ER alone is the minimum for commercial sales in India from April 2026.

items.question: Can I still buy cameras from brands that have not completed STQC certification?

children.text: As of April 2026, any CCTV brand that has not obtained STQC certification under ER-01:2024 cannot legally be sold as new product in the Indian market. Buyers should verify the certification status of any brand on the official portals (crsbis.in, stqc.gov.in) before purchasing. Existing installed equipment is a separate regulatory question — consult your legal counsel and check the latest MeitY notifications for updates.

items.question: Does STQC certification guarantee a camera cannot be hacked?

children.text: No certification can guarantee zero vulnerabilities. What STQC certification does confirm is that, at the time of testing, the product met the six Essential Requirements under ER-01:2024 — including encrypted transmission, signed firmware, and a published vulnerability-disclosure process. Regular firmware updates and network segmentation remain essential regardless of certification status.

items.question: How long does STQC certification remain valid?

children.text: Validity periods vary by certificate type and product. Always check the expiry date on the certificate itself via stqc.gov.in. In rapidly evolving firmware environments, ask vendors how frequently they re-certify after major software updates.

items.question: Where can I find the full list of STQC certified CCTV products?

children.text: The STQC Directorate publishes empanelled and certified product lists on stqc.gov.in. For BIS-ER registered products, use crsbis.in or lims.bis.gov.in. Both portals are updated periodically; always use the portal search rather than third-party aggregator lists.
